state.context:
Choose between three body notations for canlang, the AI-generated language for CRUD-centered company SaaS. Maximizing adoption governs the design, aided by economical tokens, dependable generation and low complexity. The language tools have not been built and no tokenization or agent generation/revision trials exist. Familiar wording does not demonstrate model reliability.
An operation signature has typed parameters with either by authorization or on verified ingress. Today lowercase then prefixes semicolon-delimited simple statements or opens a deeper body. Checks can stand before it and within it: observed sources contain 254 introducers, including 100 inline and 154 block forms; 34 requires are inside these blocks. Depth increases by a single space. Transaction failure discards provisional work for a require at any point, independently of then; pure read operations retain typed-return restrictions. Capitalized Given/When/Then stays at package level with Then for presentation. Authored assertions remain isolated in examples, and metadata/comments stay #/##.
A direct body avoids the recurring introducer and outdents children once without changing their relative nesting. It could save 154 wrapper lines and repeated words, while risking scope errors or production/test confusion unless examples is reserved distinctly. Keeping then avoids a rename and retains a dedicated existing parse container; its sequence/result meaning can blur execution versus BDD expectations or capitalized Then. Switching to do keeps all inline/block depth, dataflow, order, access, rollback and test scope. It may signal body execution clearly, yet sound effect-specific in reads and require generators to change their learned spelling. The rename saves 508 UTF-8 bytes across 254 markers and no lines/depth, with unmeasured model-token differences. Preservation requires full specification and a correct migration for any choice; none is proved safe by these samples or adds transaction semantics or permission. The goal is one canonical syntax rather than parallel equivalents.
Hypothetical entities and a fixture illustrate each notation without successful compilation. Weigh both benefits and potential errors, including the possibility of an unresolved preference. Earlier answers and expectations of agreement are not supplied.

examples.then_body:
scenario finish(item:Item) by=members
 require item.status==open
 then
  let selected=item.Part
  require count(selected)>0
  set item {status=done}
 examples item=fixture_item
  item.status -> item.status
  open -> done
examples.do_body:
scenario finish(item:Item) by=members
 require item.status==open
 do
  let selected=item.Part
  require count(selected)>0
  set item {status=done}
 examples item=fixture_item
  item.status -> item.status
  open -> done
examples.direct_body:
scenario finish(item:Item) by=members
 require item.status==open
 let selected=item.Part
 require count(selected)>0
 set item {status=done}
 examples item=fixture_item
  item.status -> item.status
  open -> done

body_spelling.instructions: Select the best canonical scenario-body notation after weighing the described advantages and risks.

criteria.direct: Use the scenario itself as the ordered executable container with no body-marker word.
criteria.unresolved: Leave the relative preference open because available facts do not support selecting a spelling.
criteria.do: Rename the existing container keyword to do without altering its inline or nested rules.
criteria.then: Continue using then for the current explicit execution-body container.
